utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Cont'd]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you produced a number of exhibits, D223, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, I think, and so on, reflecting what happened between June and October of 1992. Perhaps you could just have a look at one of them for me, please, D223/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can put the English version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a typed document, as we can see, and it's got a numbering system that's been put on in hand, I think. I beg your pardon. It's got a numbering system that's been typed on, 01-120/92. Can you explain the system to me, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbering system followed an order. Each new document followed an order. It would be issued the next number, and then after "slash" two digits of the year would be entered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the Croatian Community's Defence Council. Would you like to have a look, please, at Exhibit Z129, which we looked at yesterday. Now, look at this one. The number is there. But it's in hand. Do you see the number? 01-122/92. Do you see that number?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that part of the same series? is what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are -- this is numbering of two separate bodies, of which each had their own logging system. Here you can see that this was Croatian Defence Council in Busovaca, and the 10th June document is headed "Croatian Defence Council Regional Staff of Central Bosnia in Travnik." So those are two different bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I mean I can see the point about it being a different body to the extent of being a regional staff, but in fact, document 129 for the 10th of June is headed "Busovaca" as well, and the numbering system is identical in format, and that's why I wanted your help. It may relate to something in Travnik. It's an order form, we know, but it actually comes from Busovaca. Is it the same numbering system or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the same numbering system. It's a separate system. We could find similar systems with business companies and some other bodies in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you will notice, of course, that the number on Z129 for the 10th of June is number 122, and the document for the 27th of June, D223/1, is an earlier number, number 120. Well now, as to these documents that you've produced, and we might as well just stay with D223/1, there's only one signature on it, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think for all the documents we looked at yesterday, there's never a Muslim signature on any of the documents. Would that be correct? I want to deal with these matters quickly, if I can.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to review these documents quickly to see whether there were other signatures on them or not, but from what I recall from yesterday, the documents entered yesterday, I remember that there were a number of documents where I took notes, and it was not necessary for two persons to keep notes of the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that these documents weren't raised in cross-examination with witnesses with whom they might have been. I'm not in the position to take a position in relation to the documents specifically at the moment. It may be I will be before the witness is finished. Probably not, but I'll just make a couple of observations to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to these documents, there may well have been meetings to which they related, but I'm going to suggest to you, in the most general terms, that the records made were both unilateral and, in a sense, slanted. Do you accept that, slanted by being prepared by one side only?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These meetings did take place. It is not that they may have taken place. I was a participant in those meetings, and the minutes accurately reflect who attended them. They were not one-sided. They are just descriptive of what happened in those meetings. They truthfully reflected the contents of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the broadcast seems to have this witness' face blocked out. I think that must be an error, unless I'm mistaken. Perhaps it should be corrected for public purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm going to try and deal with the summer of 1992 quite shortly. The reality is, is it not, that -- the reality is that those Muslims who returned to or retained their jobs did so in subordinate or lower positions than they'd had before; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, and one cannot define it only some Muslims. All Muslims who were municipal employees were returned to their jobs, to these jobs which they held before, and I think that there are documents to support this. There are decisions, and I believe that there are also logbooks and also payrolls. You can tell that they were coming and they were receiving their salaries in jobs which they held before. Only persons who were mobilised into either the TO or the HVO were not coming, because they went to the military, and they may have been coming back for their salaries because no salaries were being paid by the military organisations at that time. And only female employees with children less than -- of ages under 7 have the right to attend to them and still receive salaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this same period of time, the late spring and summer of 1992, were barricades put up in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please specify what period does the question refer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be after the period in May, in particular. Were barricades put up?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is -- it is important to say whether it was after 10 May because I said that after that there were new barricades, and after a while they were removed, 12 or 13 days thereafter. I have already stated that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there armed patrols of HVO touring the streets?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the HVO military police and the TO military police and the civilian police all patrolled the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in particular, the HVO, was that not -- are you saying the Territorial Defence were allowed to patrol?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO military police, the HVO military police, and the civilian police patrolled the areas of the Busovaca municipality as agreed to in the documents which have been presented to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must challenge you on that. Can you explain how, in the course of the spring and summer of 1992, if it be the case, the telephone lines for Muslims were cut from time to time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were -- that the lines were cut. I don't know what the reasons for that were, but both Croats and Muslims were affected. I could not tell you anything about the technical reasons for it because I'm not a professional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 28th of May, 1992, might you have been looking at the television, a broadcast at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a long time ago. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can play just the beginning of the tape, but before we do, what do you say Mr. Kordic's role in 1992 was, if you were to have introduced him to someone? What would you have said he was?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday. I said on several occasions, that to me, the position of Mr. Dario Kordic and his status in 1992 was not fully defined but that in 1993, I perceived his role as one of a spokesman for the Croat Community in the besieged Lasva River Valley, and I know that Mr. Dario Kordic in 1992 was the vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and vice-president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not vice-president of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, Mr. Kordic was never the vice-president of the HVO. I said that after August 1992, Mr. Prlic was president of the HVO, and Mr. Anto Valenta was later appointed the vice-president of the HVO for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can just play the beginning of a tape. It's Z117. While this is coming up -- this is, I gather, 18 minutes in total. I wasn't intending to play it in full in order to save time. It's a document that I'll discuss in closing argument. If we can just have the first -- here we go.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Very little is known about the Croatian Defence Council, this is why we have come to Busovaca to ask Mr. Dario Kordic, vice-president of the Croatian Defence Council, for an interview. Our first question is precisely this: Can you explain what the Croatian Defence Council is? Obviously from the conversation we had before filming this programme, the question you asked in private, I realised that there was much surrounding the Croatian Defence Council that was unclear, especially in Sarajevo and in those areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina which effectively have no information from other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just pause it there for the time being. Now, Your Honour, I'm entirely in the Court's hands. You can see it's a good quality tape and we have a transcript of it. But it will take 18 minutes to watch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there some part you want to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I think, first of all, I must ask the witness if he saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this yourself?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are a number of passages in it of potential relevance to argument. I can point them out to the Chamber to save time or I can have it played, but I am acutely aware of the pressure that we are all under about time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we don't want to have it played because of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be better to leave it to argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In which case, I shan't address it at all at the moment; we'll just come to it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just this please. Can you help us with how it could be that Mr. Kordic was introduced as the vice-president of the HVO or is the truth that that's exactly what he was?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say to the Trial Chamber that I was not -- that I have not been able to read the transcript, but as I scanned through the first -- through the first page, and it is the reporter that introduces Dario Kordic as the vice-president of the Croatian Defence Council, but I did not find that Mr. Kordic confirmed that. I do not exclude the possibility of that happening, but I just have not been able to read through the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. In the autumn of 1992, September, there were moves to relocate various offices including Mr. Kordic's to Travnik, to make Travnik a Croatian centre for Central Bosnia. You were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of such activities, that the office of the vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the office of the vice-president of the HDZ-BiH, and I believe the offices of the government for Central Bosnia, would be transferred to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Travnik was a known Muslim majority area.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that in Travnik, from what I know, large numbers of Croats, Muslims, and Serbs lived in Travnik, about 26.000 Croats. It was a multi-ethnic town and now it is a city where there is parity of the Croats and Muslims, each making about 50 per cent of the population currently and it's a seat of the canton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just this, in 1992, in this part of 1992, the confidence of the HVO was such that having taken Busovaca over, it was felt by Mr. Kordic that he could move and set up government in a place where it would be bound to upset the Muslims to do so. Would that not be correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept the -- this as you put it, that he took over something like that. I think that this was a logical activity to set up some civilian bodies which the -- which would enable the entire defence to be affected. I will only remind you that following this period, there was the Lasva Valley that was in danger of falling after Jajce, falling to the Bosnian Serbs. And that the agreement was made to defend Travnik, and Travnik was defended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, you've told us about Mr. Kordic knowing him before all this happened. At the time you knew him, he was a committed communist, I think, when you first knew him.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot qualify him, and I don't think that I would describe him as committed. The job openings at that time were such that you had to be a member of the communist party in order to aspire to certain job levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was an active member, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have too much information about that, but I know that he was not a committed communist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that then?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We lived in a town for which you could not tell that it was full of committed communists. Those who were known to everyone, and the others, you could say, were just regular people, regular members of the Communist Party who had to join the party in order to get certain jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was then able to rise very rapidly in the HDZ in Busovaca, and indeed the HVO then, as we've seen, took Busovaca over, and he rose and was continuing to rise in authority throughout 1992. That's a fair picture of the man, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to point out again I disagree with the term to "take over," that the HVO "took over" Busovaca. Second, in the HDZ hierarchy, and this was a party that was only beginning to get established, it was being established through various branches and people joining in, it is not as if people joined it in order to use it as a stepladder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We must remember that the incident that justified the action in May was an incident that happened at an HVO checkpoint that had been put up without warning in the direction of Kaonik. That's right, isn't it? It was an HVO checkpoint where the first incident occurred, which was relied upon by Kordic and others for what they subsequently did; correct? It's in your own summary.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: That is not correct. I can only testify before this Trial Chamber regarding civilian affairs, organisation, management of roads. And as to how this incident took place, what happened, I don't know. I just don't have enough information to be able to testify about it before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may not have enough information to testify about it, but you had enough information to say, at paragraph 36 of your summary, that there was an altercation at an HVO checkpoint. So I think you -- did you know that or did somebody tell you that, that it was an HVO checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I was very clear about this in my testimony before this Court. I do not think there is any need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to deal with things overall, Mr. Kordic's ascendancy in Busovaca and elsewhere continued right up until mid-April of 1993, when, to everyone's surprise, the Muslims put up rather a better defence than anybody had expected and indeed became the superior force. That's about the truth, isn't it, overall?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall repeat that I'm not an expert on military matters. I really cannot answer it, how strong any party was. I simply cannot say. I'm not an expert. I do not know military rules or, rather, that military logic. I was a soldier in the JNA in 1983 and 1984, but I earned no rank in that army, yet I was perhaps the man with the highest education in that army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to move on very rapidly then if that's your answer. Were you, by any chance, present at a reception given in Busovaca shortly before Christmas of 1992 when a man called de Boer was present, an international monitor? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: International monitor de Boer, I recall that he was not an international monitor. He was the commander of the Dutch unit of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you do.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I just don't know what reception you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At such receptions would Mr. Kordic be dressed as and addressed as a lieutenant colonel or a colonel?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I communicated with people from the municipal administration, communicated with ECMM and with the British Battalion of UNPROFOR and the Dutch Battalion in the UNPROFOR, but now I cannot recall that Mr. Kordic was ever present during those contacts. As far as I recall, I was never present at any meeting together with Mr. Kordic. As far as I can remember, of course, because it was seven or eight years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just help us in general. Did he dress as a colonel and like to be called "Colonel"?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with military ranks and what it looked like, but I never saw any rank insignia on Mr. Kordic's clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's really the case, is it, that you're not familiar at all, despite having lived through a war and worked in the government offices, you're not familiar with military ranks? Don't you know what a colonel is?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember the ranks from the time when I served the JNA but now they're quite different. Right at this moment, I have no idea about ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on much further, just this business of Mr. Kordic going to the front line. I think you were there, were you, yourself, or you saw him going? What's the position?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Where do you -- are you asking me if I saw him at the front line or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he went off to help the troops at the front lines.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see him go there. I only heard him say to the soldiers that he was inviting them to go defend Jajce and to volunteer for that, that he would go too. I testified about that before the Court and I think we're now repeating ourselves. I was never at the front line in Jajce, and I do not know when those volunteers went to that front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'd like your help with is this, as a local residence -- incidently, roughly how many people lived in the town of Busovaca itself? Not the overall area, the town of Busovaca. How many thousand?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the broader area, what is meant by the town, that is, the municipal boundaries of the town, and they are pretty wide around Busovaca, so almost 4.000 inhabitants live in the town of Busovaca, that is, in the part that is officially called the locality, the settlement of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That includes outlying villages and hamlets. The town itself is actually very small, isn't it, just a couple of thousand people?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how shall I put it? I think that the boundary follows the road up to some 2.5 kilometres from the centre of the town in one direction and about two kilometres in the other direction, and it does not include villages. One could perhaps refer to them as suburbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I just want the Judges, you see, to have from you a picture of quite how small and intimate really this -- it's little more than a big village, isn't it, Busovaca? Would that be about a fair description?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: In light of the conditions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are about 110 municipal seats in BH, and this one was the 80th ranking -- the 80th amongst the municipal seats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, just one sentence. There is one fact I should like to point out. As I have already testified, I did not live in Busovaca until August 1992, but in a village some 10 kilometres away from Busovaca. It was wartime, and I had to go through several barricades to reach home, so that after work, I would either go home or I was completing the construction of my new house. So that wasn't really wise to all the events as the Prosecutor seems to imply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm only dealing with the things about which you were aware, and one of them seems to be that Mr. Kordic was going to provide some help for the troops at the front line. Can you explain to me, please, as a local resident, why a spokesman, if that's what he was, would be able to stimulate the troops? You see, just so that I can finish the point, we're all familiar with political leaders and military leaders inspiring their troops, but can you explain how a spokesman can do that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I'm referring to 1992 when soldiers were invited to go to Jajce to defend it. And I said that in 1993, as far as [indiscernible], Mr. Kordic was the spokesman for the besieged population in the Lasva Valley, and I cannot really go into it why the soldiers trust Mr. Kordic. He was not their commander. But the citizens of Busovaca, soldiers, not only in Busovaca, trusted Mr. Dario Kordic. They trusted his words. They knew he was a man of integrity, a principled man, and I have already testified about this to this Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's truth about it is in 1992, you and other Croats with success or comparative success coming your way were enthused by notions of the wider Croatia, you were enthused by nations of the old Banovina; true?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified about that too. There were such ideas here and there. In a democratic society, nobody can stop anyone from voicing his political views. But after the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I never heard it voiced officially. There may have been an individual idea, but a little bit, but officially, no, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to move on to the incident in January of 1993. Can you explain at all why several defence -- well, what was the date of this incident in January, 1993, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already testified about that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat that you've already testified. If counsel asks you a question and it is overbearing and repetitious, he will be stopped. But otherwise, could you just answer shortly, please, to his questions. You were asked what the date was. Just give us the date.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 24th of January, 1993. It was the incident when Petrovic, an HVO military policeman, was killed at a checkpoint in Kacuni. I heard while being in my house some gunfire around 1600 on the 24th of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were there any other incidents in January of 1993 that you can tell us about that happened before that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I was told not to repeat, that I have already testified about this. I will not repeat that once again, but on the 20th or 21st of January, 1993, I heard that there was an incident at a checkpoint in Kacuni when Mr. Ignac Kostroman, who was the secretary of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was stopped there and as far as I could understand, he was not allowed to go through to his home in Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this happened on the 24th or the 25th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To be fair to the witness, he said in evidence in chief that it was the 20th or the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I noticed without comment that that's the date that he gave, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, what is your recollection about the date, please? What is your recollection about the date of the incident at the checkpoint at Kacuni? It's your evidence.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said it was the 20th or the 21st of January, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to bother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is very unsatisfactory. The question was asked by Mr. Sayers. We've heard about an incident that occurred on the 20th or the 21st in Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not waste time. We are a professional body of Judges. We do not need this kind of detail. We can see what's happening with the witness. We'll make our own mind up about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then please, Mr. Grubesic, just tell us the detail of what happened to Mr. Kostroman. That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had heard that he had been stopped there. I do not have any other information about the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you told us that things happened after that to certain premises. To what premises did things happen?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During that period of time, sometime between the 20th and the 23rd, I'm not sure of the date, a large number of Muslim premises in Busovaca were damaged, damaged not destroyed, and several Croat shops were also damaged, but there was a larger number of Muslim shops damaged. That is, their window shops were broken, hand grenades had been thrown into some of these outlets, but none of them were demolished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why were Muslim premises, as you would describe it, damaged? At this time in January, why, can you help us, were prominent Muslim citizens arrested at this time, in this small town?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about arrests made at that time, and I really cannot fathom why these shops were damaged. What were the reasons for that, one could, of course, make guesses, but I really do not know what the true reason is behind that, and I cannot comment about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the murder? You haven't mentioned the murder about the man, Delija. What was that all to do with?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Delija's murder, but now I cannot tell you because I do not know what were the circumstances or when it happened. Whether it was before the 25th of January or after the 25th of January, I really do not know. What I do know only is that it did take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it rumoured to be connected to Mr. Kordic or to Mr. Kostroman or to both?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of such comments. I shall say only one sentence: The situation at that time was very confused and it was very difficult to obtain any information in wartime. And I think war anywhere, it is best to stay put at home and not move about, especially at night. I think this applies to war in general. So I spent most of the time with my family. I would go to work and come back home from work. In wartime, the situation is very difficult and very confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, you're claiming amnesia or never having known of events when it's inconvenient, aren't you? That's the truth, because you know perfectly well in your small town what happened to lead to both the bombings and the killing.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If something happened three streets away from here, we wouldn't know what had happened there, would we, because we are not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to just deal with a couple of particular matters. May the witness have Exhibit 461, please. It's a sealed exhibit so it shouldn't go on the ELMO. It may be sealed, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is apparently sealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just look, yourself, please, at -- the entries are all dated, and since it's sealed, can you just read it to yourself. All right? Go, for example, to the 26th of January, our page 5. Have you read the entry for the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were staying in your house, so you may not have seen or heard everything, but is that entry, as an example, an accurate entry of what was happening in January of 1993 in your small town?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will remember that I already said that with my wife, who was expecting, I went to the shelter on the 24th, that I spent several days there and never left that shelter because there was a lot of gunfire and shelling. So it was very dangerous to go out of the shelter. I cannot give you any precise, that is, any information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well then one more short extract. Come back a couple of pages. A very short extract, bottom of our page 3. I don't know where it is in the original. 21st, 22nd, and 23rd of January. Read it to yourself. Is that an accurate account of the 21st, 22nd, and 23rd?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any of the things indicated here, and the only thing I can say is that I realised, at a later stage, that the Muslims had begun leaving Busovaca. And I did not know about that, nor did I know reasons about it. It was only later that I found out that it had happened. And perhaps just one more comment. From what I can see, this document was written on the 12th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not challenging -- you tell us you didn't hear it, but you're not challenging that what's said there for the 21st, 22nd, and 23rd of January might well be true. You accept it might well be true, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I did not hear something or see something, then I cannot say anything about it, can I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 3rd of February, Mr. Jennings. I'll just deal with this very briefly. Could you look at this map, please, which I can make available. It's 2781.2. I'll show the usher the bit to put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a census document, Defence 116/1, that the Chamber may wish to remind itself of, and that document I can also make available to the witness in a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The position is this, is it not: The place marked -- sorry. Is there a problem with the map, Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The map shows the area between Kacuni and something marked as Donje Polje; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I see on the screen, that particular area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The colours don't come out particularly well, but you can see on the original that there runs north -- well, there runs from Donje Polje down to Kacuni, a river, and it crosses the road some distance to the north-west of Kacuni, the little bridge there. We can actually see it. If you can see it, you might point it out with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the bridge. You've given evidence about Muslim houses and Muslim occupation of Polje or Donje Polje, and I can hand the census form to you, but the evidence we've heard is this: that along the road from that bridge in the direction of Donje Polje, there are houses, I think on either side, or there were houses on either side. That would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the way from Kacuni to Busovaca, there are houses on both sides more or less. They may be slightly scattered perhaps, they're not close to one another, not wall to wall, but yes, there are houses all along the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The census document that shows a nil return for Muslims deals not with Donje Polje but Polje, and that same census documents also allows for the existence of eight Yugoslavs and seven other ethnic group inhabitants. You can have the document if you want to. The evidence that we've heard is that along that road, houses that happened to have or had four-sided roofs were being visited by men with HVO uniforms or HVO insignia and were being set on fire. Now, that's the evidence. You're not able to tell us yourself, are you, to which particular part of this overall area the census relating to Polje relates? You have the document to look at, of course, if you want to. Have mine for speed.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can see in this document and as far as I can remember, it is accurate as far as Polje is concerned. So as far as I understood, 729 inhabitants, 5 Serbs, no Muslims, and 709 Croats, 8 Yugoslavs, and 7 others. I believe that these figures are accurate figures reflecting the population structure in Polje in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't know along that road from Donje Polje to Kacuni where the boundary is, and I'm going to suggest to you that there were houses along that road that belonged to Muslims and that they were indeed being destroyed in February 1993 by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Were you asking me something? Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm suggesting to you -- you've given evidence about habitation.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: I don't know how accurate I can point to things on the map, but the bridge that I have pointed out --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What about the bridge?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This [indicates]. There was an incident on this bridge when the military policeman Petrovic was killed on the 25th of January -- no, 24th of January, 1993. The settlement of Polje starts by this creek which is called Babjak. I'm going to point it on the map. Here in the direction of Busovaca, that is where the village of Polje runs [indicates]. Up to here is the village of Kacuni, to this point on the road. This is where Kacuni and Polje border each other. And from here, almost until the entrance to Busovaca, there's Polje and there's some additional villages there [indicates]. There's not -- there is no single Muslim home alongside the road. I can almost tell you, house by house, who owns it. I went to school there, I knew these people, and I could name all these --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. The point you've pointed to is the junction of the two villages that indeed fits with what -- the evidence we've heard, so that's fine. I needn't ask you any more about that. Thank you. I think I've got very little more to ask you. You were in charge of passes or you had the right to issue passes in the war for the passage of property and goods. That was a method of raising taxes, wasn't it, passes for the passage of goods?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The passes for passage of goods were not being charged. There was no charge for them, but they could be used by the tax authority to follow the traffic of goods. And Mr. Glavocevic was in charge of this, and I could only do it in his absence which, I believe, never actually happened, that I signed any of such passes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did either of you charge the issue of passes?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was a service in the municipal government in charge of that. I think for the passage, there was a charge for the passage of people. I think the fee was around one German mark per person, but I was not directly involved in this. I know that there was a tax, maybe 10 or 20 marks for the passage of goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two other questions. Why were men of military age arrested and detained in Kaonik in early 1993, please, Muslim men of military age? What conceivable reason was there for doing that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know why this happened. I said where I was during that period. There are several possible reasons for it. One is probably that they were captured with weapons so that the prisoner could be put somewhere. So in that sense --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were Muslim men of military age rounded up and imprisoned in Busovaca, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact reason why this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did Mr. Kordic take up headquarters in the PTT building and do so with all the accoutrements of being a military officer, uniformed and armed guards. You were there, why did it happen?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Kordic did not move any headquarters of his into the PTT building. I think that at that time, the basement -- the PTT basement was a fairly secure place, secure from shelling, and I think that the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade headquarters were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why would he be there in military uniform, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there during that period. I never entered the PTT building during that period when the headquarters was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain to us, please, why there were only 30-odd Muslims left in Busovaca by February of 1994. They were driven out, weren't they, all the others?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that those are accurate data. Let me give you one piece of information. There are about 30 Muslim families in my neighbourhood, and I know that they stay there until September or October 1993, they stayed in their homes. And that with the influx of fresh refugees who had been driven out of Zenica, these displaced people forcibly pushed those Muslims out of their homes and moved in and gave them documents allowing them to enter their homes which they had left in Zenica. So the information, data for this period are not accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a Croatian passport, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the passport of Bosnia and Herzegovina and I have the passport of the Republic of Croatia. I have a dual citizenship. I have the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, according to the law, I also have the right to the citizenship of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not, of course, going to ask you any questions about the awful tragedy of your parents and I'm not in a position to deal with the detail. Just help us, have you at any time spoken to the investigators of this Tribunal about those circumstances or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never invited by the investigators of this Tribunal to talk about this. I only gave a statement in the police station in Busovaca in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I want to take the witness back to something which he said in the latter part of his examination-in-chief. It is in relation to Mr. Kordic's encouraging the soldiers to defend Jajce and he said Mr. Kordic said words to the effect, "I will go with you to the front lines not as a soldier but as a politician." I want to ask the witness whether that was the direct speech of Mr. Kordic, in other words, was that -- were those his exact words, or do they represent your understanding of what he would, in fact, be doing were he to go to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exact words of Mr. Kordic were, "We have to defend Jajce and I will go with you to defend Jajce." And the rest is my understanding of it in that context. I never heard from anyone, nor did I see that Mr. Kordic was in any place with the weapon in his hands so I drew a conclusion that he would go up there as a politician. That was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just two or three questions, Mr. President. I wonder if I could show Mr. Grubesic one of the documents that he was asked about, Z78 and Z78A. Re-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, you were shown this document and asked some questions about it by the Prosecution and certain propositions were put to you regarding the conclusions that are to be drawn from the fact that Mr. Kordic signed it. As you can see from the introductory part of this document, it says, "In accordance with the order of the Ministry of National Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and there's a stamp on the Croatian original. Sir, could you identify that stamp? It appears to be in Cyrillic, and I can't read it, but does that look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I am re-analysing this document, I can indeed see, I am referring to the document itself, that the document was issued by the -- in accordance with the order of the Ministry of the National Defence of the Republic of BH. And as far as a seal is concerned, it was done in two alphabets. The better one is in Cyrillic. These were the usual prewar seals in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so both in the Cyrillic. It says the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Busovaca municipality, the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence. And then it also has a prewar coat of arms in the middle. That is done both in Cyrillic and in Roman alphabets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one final question. The Ministry of National Defence of the republic, was that a military institution or a civilian institution?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a civilian institution at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which would correspond to the Ministry of Defence, and here it was called People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document, Mr. Usher, and there's one other document that I would like to have put on the ELMO, and I've highlighted a parenthetical phrase. I'd just like the witness to read this slowly in his own language and get an accurate translation of this document, Z111 and Z111A, for which there are various translations provided to us by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let's just have it read in the original language, sir, and see what it says. And this is from paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The language I've highlighted in between the brackets, and I've highlighted it in yellow.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the entire paragraph 3 but just the part in parenthesis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All employees of the administrative bodies of the Busovaca Municipal Assembly, as well as the employees of all companies and institutions in the Busovaca municipality area, the employees of the Busovaca public security station," in parenthesis, "except for the employees of the police station who do not wish to place themselves under the HVO command."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grubesic. That's just fine. I'm through with that exhibit. Thank you. Then the last exhibit I'd like you to look at was the exhibit that was under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So please don't put this on the ELMO, but if you'd just show it to the witness. Thank you. Exhibit Z461. And just for the Trial Chamber's information, there's an ancillary exhibit that I'm sure the Trial Chamber remembers, Z461A, which is a rather more chronologically concentrated version of this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you two questions, sir. In connection with the entry --

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry. I only received a copy in the English language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. My error. Thank you. If you could just turn to the entry for January the 20th and the 21st. Is there any mention at all of anyone being stopped at a checkpoint by ABiH troops? Any mention of Mr. Kostroman being stopped or indeed of Mr. Kordic being there? Could you just inform us of that, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To look at 20th and 21st. Very well. I'll need a little bit of time to be able to read through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To save some time, Your Honour, if I could just put the proposition to the witness, and if the Prosecution has any observations, I'd be more than delighted to hear from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no mention of anyone being stopped at any checkpoint, Mr. Kostroman or Mr. Kordic, on the 20th or 21st in this document that appears to be generated by the head of the Muslim police station in Kacuni. Would you agree with that from your scanning the document, Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I scan through it, I cannot find any mention of the incident of anyone being stopped at the checkpoint in Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Last question. On page 3 of the English version, there's a mention of the murder of Mr. Delija, about which questions were asked of you by the Prosecution. Could you just tell us whether you found that, sir. I believe it's towards the end of January 20th.

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is there any contention made in the document that was prepared several weeks after this incident of any rumours, scuttlebutt, hearsay, gossip, things of that type, that connected this incident with Mr. Kordic in any way, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKO GRUBESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, it would be convenient to take the break now, unless there's something you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a couple of minutes to discuss the protective measures for the next witness very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't have the document. I thought I did, but I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Trial Chamber's permission, we can -- if we are going to discuss it before the break, we need to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a few minutes to go through the particulars of this witness and could we go back into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, you're on -- the Court will allow you to look at your summary from time to time during your testimony, but I do not think it is really necessary for you to refer to it. You can answer your questions falling back on your memory but, of course, you can refer to it if need be. The Court has already heard a great deal about the historical background so we do not have to go into it. Just one sentence. From the point of view of you, the inhabitants of the municipality, when did some more noteworthy, some grave misunderstandings begin between the Muslims and Croats in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: In our municipality, these misunderstandings began when the Yugoslav People's Army requested the evacuation of the barracks or, rather, after the war had broken out in Croatia officially, and weapons were being requested to be taken to the territory of the Republic of Croatia and other places so as to wage war. It is a fact that the Croat people, that is, or I can say about myself, in Croatia, I have a sister in Osijek, for instance, and Osijek, at that time, was under fierce shelling and destroyed. She used to work in the hospital. The hospital was badly destroyed, and every time she went to work, it was a hazardous business. So I had personal reasons to be concerned about the movement of those convoys because some of them were also going to that particular area in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was about to say, as to those convoys, with there other villages with other inhabitants of the municipality, you also participated in those protests personally to prohibit, to stop the passage of weapons to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, I personally approved that, and I supported it insofar as I could do it, of course. However, it is a fact that the Muslim side was not concerned about it, it simply showed no interest, and the Serb side, I mean, those who were in Busovaca still. So that was one of the first misunderstandings between the Croat and the Muslim communities. They were inactive. They paid no attention to the fact that the Croat community was concerned about this; that it was insisting on the evacuation of the barracks; that the JNA had no business to be there; that the Croat population in Busovaca was a minority population; therefore, there was no reason for them to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So if I understand, this rift between the communities began first because of the war in Croatia and also your views and the preparations that would -- then in Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it? That was another factor that you could not agree about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, people in some higher political offices understood the situation, but I couldn't really have a full grasp of the situation. The situation was rather confused. But basically one could see that there was an aspiration that everything was leading to chaos, to disarray. One could not rely on anything with any degree of certainty, especially since some conflicts had already begun in Sarajevo. There was no communication with Sarajevo at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. We shall move step by step. Only will you please wait for my answer to be interpreted into the official languages of the Tribunal to facilitate the work of the interpreters. It will be very difficult to say who said what unless we make a break. Okay. I believe we have described, in a couple of sentences, the situation in which the Croat, that is the minority population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, accounting for only 17.4 per cent, found themselves in. A great deal has already been said here and the Court knows about the attitude of the Croats who got in the referendum. However, if there are any questions about this you can answer that, but we can move on. In spite of the referendum and in spite of the fact that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had become an autonomous and independent state, could that state stand on its own two feet; that is, did the central government ever begin to function with regard to the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, never. That is, those conflicts which were taking place around Sarajevo blocked completely the entrance, the access to Sarajevo. I know this from accounts of drivers, those who were busy with payments, who had to take money to and from the municipalities, that they would be intercepted by Chetniks, threatening them with murders, seizing their cars, and so on and so forth, so that the blockade was complete. And all the funds, all the central funds which were in Sarajevo and other central administration which was in Sarajevo did not function at all, especially with regard to the municipalities. So the municipalities somehow had to fend for themselves. The municipalities had to become states, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If anything turns on this, you will be asked some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, just one question more about this. The Court already knows about how the whole system fell into pieces -- fell to pieces, but life had to be organised in your municipality because life goes on regardless of the problems in the state, but municipality -- the municipal government organised the whole life, public health, education, finance, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was a period of time when we had to think and take some decisions, to talk to other municipalities to see how and what to organise it all. Namely, one had to organise the work of schools, because the school year was coming up; to organise the health; welfare; the work of medical institutions; to organise the payment of pensions, because the pension fund was also in Sarajevo. There was absolutely no chance of these people getting their pensions from there. So in municipalities or specifically in the municipality of Busovaca, since the payments had been cut off, all the money was kept in Busovaca. That is, the municipal government then decided that the funds should be distributed and to finance the communal needs; that is, the public institutions, health care institutions, public utilities, and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, to finance from these funds all these -- all walks of life in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the imminent danger of war, the Municipal Assembly ceased to function at some point sometime in early April 1992, and the Crisis Staff was set up, consisting of members of all the parliamentary parties, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff continue to try to organise life in the municipality? However, in those chaotic times, did it succeed or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not really sure how it functioned, because I simply had no say, nor did I have any information about the operation of the staff, especially after the shelling. For a while, we never came to work. (redacted) 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) All I heard was that this Crisis Staff was not really performing very well, that they were inefficient, that they had problems, but I really do not know much about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I suppose you were aware that some agreements had been reached with the JNA about the evacuation of the JNA, about the location of -- dislocation of, because they were in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. They had three barracks with large depots. (redacted) there was a huge barracks, and people were saying that the whole house might blow-up if this went on fire, and the situation was very tense among the population. Everybody was very anxious as to what would happen to those barracks, whether the conflict would break out straight away, whether it would be resolved in some peaceful manner. So the situation was very tense. At night, people put out their lights very early or, rather, nobody went to bed because people were afraid. There was sporadic gunfire around the barracks. So the situation was like that all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose that this collective anxiety and this tension spread especially after the bombing of Busovaca on the 26th of April by the JNA air force. There were fires and a lot of destruction had taken place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. Fear culminated at that time because nobody believed before that they would bomb it like that, that everything would be on fire, that there would be these terrible explosions. That is, I'm trying to portray the situation. I have never before experienced any bombing. And it was the culmination, horrible culmination, because everything was in flames, and the power was cut off, telephones were cut off, and there was chaos in the town because we didn't know whether the bombing would happen again. The planes flew over us the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness DE, we've heard a great deal of evidence in this case, as you appreciate. It's been going on for more than a year. Could you confine yourself to simply answering the questions, and if you'll do, that we'll get on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, you heard it from His Honour. The Court has indeed learned a great many details about this, so we do not have to do it any more. However, in this chaotic time, sometime in May 1992, in early May 1992, the tension between the Croat and the Muslim community in Busovaca culminated. You were not there yourself, but just in a sentence, what do you know about that? What is it that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: You mean in relation to the barracks and the takeover of the barracks? Well, I did not take part in this; I only heard. In the wake of it, I heard that there was a problem with the Kaonik barracks. I heard that in a nearby coffee shop; that is, it was quite a large coffee shop, and it was full of Muslim troops before that, and they were discussing the takeover of that barracks and the distribution of it 50/50. I do not really know any details about that. But there was some altercation and some gunfire, and a young man, a 21-year-old man was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. The Court knows all that. Thank you. But did you hear, perhaps, if it was only locals who had turned up or were there some people from outside the municipality? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I was told that there were also some people from outside the municipality, some people who were unknown in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that atmosphere on one of those days, the HVO in the municipality of Busovaca was founded. It was provisional measures, measures to organise life in the area. You also had certain duties to perform in the -- in that civilian body which ran the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We already said what you did, so we do not have to repeat that. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted), but did you receive any assistance from central government, was it possible to try to -- coordinate the authorities throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, no way. We were simply left to our own devices. We could not expect assistance from anywhere because the situation was growing more complex day in day out so that we simply had to rely on ourselves, try to do whatever we could do and try to organise somehow that retched life we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted). I did not ever see him come to work, only in passing when he was talking to his men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, where was he at that time? What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I should say in the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Could you tell the Court, I mean, we do not have to repeat it unless so required, but the municipal government had to ensure the health care and pensions and food supplies and schools and so on and so forth so there is no need to go on back into that and waste time. So just one sentence about it. As of May, this municipal civilian work of the HVO continued the work of the former municipal authority, that is, the organisation of the overall life in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Tell us, please, you worked with the same people for years. You've known one another for a long time. After May 1992 when the civilian HVO took over, assumed the responsibility for the situation in the municipality, have you ever heard that all of you, all of you employed there, Muslims and Croats and everybody else, had to take an oath of allegiance or sign your loyalty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, I never had to do it nor did anybody ever tell me to do that, nor were we instructed to do so. We were told to do as you did before and just treat everybody equally. The civil servants have to be polite and attend to all the needs of all the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you were required to demonstrate professional attitude?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted). Did any of them have to take the oath of allegiance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, I never heard about that, never heard about that. As far as I know, they were not requested to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, under the new job systemisation in the municipal government after May 1992, who was the only one who formally lost a job, regardless of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Asim Sunulahpasic lost his job formally or it was agreed, but it was agreed that he went back to the Vatrostalna factory where he worked before. All of them kept their jobs. (redacted) (redacted) for the TO and the BH army. But once a month, (redacted) and there was no problem. They would, nevertheless, get their salaries for that month. And it was like that until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So formally speaking, they were still (redacted) payroll although in practical terms they were in the units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, especially men. They were all in the units but that was the understanding, no problem, let's just have them report and they would get their salaries so they were paid regularly. There were, I think, 72 people on the payroll in November 1992. They all got their salaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, since we are talking about the organisation of work in the municipal government, have you ever heard or, rather, did you ever hear that there was ever any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness is following the summary very closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you close the summary up, please. And since this is -- Mr. Naumovski, since this is very much in dispute, perhaps you would not lead on this evidence. Perhaps the witness could give her own evidence. What was the attitude towards the Muslim employees by the HVO municipal government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are getting French. Now we seem to be all right. Could you start again, please, Witness DE?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I'm saying that the attitude of the authorities towards all the employees was the same, there was no difference.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted)-- and received their pay, their salaries regularly, even though they did not come to work regularly because they worked for the army of BH or the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no further questions from Your Honours, may I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was part of the -- my own question, and I was helped out by the Trial Chamber. Did you ever hear that there was a direct or indirect discrimination against people of other ethnic groups in any of the services of the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: You see, there were very few of us there, that is, towards the end of 1992 and early 1993. There were very few of us working there because the situation was difficult in general, and it was not very safe. And I believe in respect of the municipal government services, special care was -- that special attention was taken to also consider the Muslim employees because we all needed to work and survive somehow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, in late November or in December of 1992, (redacted) (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of those, how many were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: There were seven Muslims. And as I said, they all received their salaries, some even got bonuses like Ms. Nasiha Neslanovic who had additional work. She had additional areas to clean. Because we had fewer people coming in to work, we would distribute the entire workload among those who came. So they, for instance, had to clean the land office rooms, that was 120 square metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have to go into all this detail. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we should avoid further details so I thought that we may enter the -- tender as an exhibit the list of all the work done by all the employees at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you want to do that, do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply thought that we would put it in the record and the document will speak for itself. I will have no further questions of the document. Can the usher please assist me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this document to be distributed, out of 72 municipal employees who were working there in January 1993, how many of them were receiving salaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: As far as the employees are concerned, the 19 that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I meant all departments.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: There were 72 including all those who only occasionally showed up for work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of that total number, how many Muslims were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I believe that there were 25, 26. I cannot give you the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be marked D 233/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, is this the document, if you could just scan it very briefly, is this the logbook of all employees and their times and who worked when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, that is that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. No need to go any further into it. As you said, you tried to do what you could to organise a life there, but also to have an open ear to the wishes of the citizenry; in other words, not to impose certain views on certain -- on citizens. So if a citizen came to get some kind of a certificate or other document from the municipal services, could they choose what type of letterhead they would get?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. After we had reached the agreement, after the provisional government was established in Busovaca, very soon thereafter, we produced this documents which had two different letterheads or headings; one with the lilies, one with the Herceg-Bosna seal. Because some people asked, depending on what they needed it for, they asked for different types of documents so the Muslim citizens and Croat citizens could get which ever type of document they wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who decided which type of letterhead was going to be used on which document, the official or the party that came for it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: The party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also worked on the organisation of the school system. There were a number of schools in the Busovaca school system. At that time, the school curriculum was not fully defined. There was still the old curriculum but -- from the old state, but also the HVO in Mostar had its own curriculum. Were there problems relating to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: At the beginning of the school year, we called all the school principals, I think that the head of the municipality did so, and a meeting was held. And we said that the curriculum should be adjusted, that the Serbian authors should be omitted, that -- and other adjustments should be made. So at the level of the Mostar government and also the Central Bosnian level, such meetings were organised and the school principals discussed the adjustments to the school curriculum. The curriculum from the government in Mostar was such that we could agree with the Muslim counterparts specifically in language, that they could use their own name for their mother tongue, the Bosniak. At that time they did not exist. Also, to study particular authors and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these agreements -- regarding these agreements, those who agreed were members of both ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. There were three elementary schools. There was one in Kacuni where the principal wore the Muslim because the population was majority Muslim, and there was one in Busovaca and one in Kaonik. They would sit down together and hold joint meetings. There were no particular objections except that they needed to sit down and work out those curricula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in Kacuni the principal was a Muslim, but did Croats also teach there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Until the first conflict on the 24th, 25th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, January 1993. That is correct. In fact, my colleague who used to teach music there, her name is Dragica Miocevic, a couple of days before moved across the lines because she said that there was a lot of concentration of soldiers and that conflict would break out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Dragica Miocevic was one of the non-Muslim teachers who worked there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. She also lived there and she worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did what she say would happen indeed happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. The very next day, we had that terrible night where all this shooting could be heard coming from Kacuni, when there was a mass exodus of people from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those days before this event, that is, before your conversation with your friend, had you heard of another incident in the Kacuni area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I heard that many people were being stopped at the checkpoint in Kacuni. Among others, Ignac Kostroman, who several days before was on his way home in Kresevo, had been stopped, and I heard that he was verbally abused. I think I also heard about that on the Radio Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were no eyewitness to this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No. I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the ceasefire was established in February and until April, it was relatively calm, if I can put it that way. You continued to work in your job, as did all other people in those municipal agencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. The situation had calmed down. We could even go to Split for food. The permits were being issued. Some of the male employees were withdrawn from the checkpoints, and permits were issued for passage of goods and foodstuffs and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in Travnik in 1993 -- sorry, in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I think this was close to Easter 1993. A new Muslim offensive was launched. I think we were attacked from the direction of Kula. My brother was wounded there, so I know about this very well. There was terrible shooting and people were being killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
