utterances.text: Their Honours have had plenty of opportunity to hear that. I wanted to limit the questioning to what is closer to you. How was that reflected in your work? Were people able to come to work due to shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: It was very unsafe to come to work, and shells were falling also around the municipal building. Many people did not show up, only those whose apartments and houses were close by. I believe that I did not come to work for about 15, 20 days, and (redacted) because she was very close by. And in -- for a long period during 1993, (redacted) (redacted) .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this also reflected on the payment of salaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No. Everything was blocked on all sides. People were being killed. The defence lines which had also been established in town. Shells were falling throughout the territory of the municipality, including the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you just tell the Trial Chamber: You said that Croats did not come to work, as well as Muslims, because of the difficulties in travelling. But all the way to May, were there still any Muslim employees in the municipal agencies in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. Alma Hodzic was still around in May [sic] 1993. She was the last one to leave. She was a very fine young woman and very hard worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So up until May [sic] 1993, there were still Muslim employees there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, but very few of us showed up to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. There was a war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. Many people were unable to come. We had shortened our business days, four to five hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just one point for the Trial Chamber. Why did the population -- what did the population of Busovaca live on? What were the sources of food supplies and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: We were -- the blockade was total, so it was through the humanitarian aid, through UNHCR, the Caritas. That is how the humanitarian aid arrived, and it was distributed to all people living in the Busovaca area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was looking at the transcript. When you spoke about Alma Hodzic, and I asked you that too, you said she worked until September. However, page 3 -- I think it was said "May."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: That is a mistake, because I have documents to support that, that it was until September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So September 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said to the Trial Chamber that there was shelling, that there were hard times for any kind of organisation of life. You said that you were close to the town of Busovaca, that you also had experiences from your village of Kaonik. Can you tell us, among the civilian population, that is, among the citizens of Busovaca municipality, were there many casualties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: There weren't that many, but there were frequent shellings. Sometimes there would be for ten days in a row. I could not let my children go out for ten days in a row. Children are curious, but I was afraid. It was safer for me to stay in the house. But that was very difficult for the children. That made them very nervous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this confined space in which you lived, let's say from April 1993 until the spring of 1994, do you have any knowledge of the total number of casualties in general?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we had evidence about this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Several questions about Dario Kordic, with whom, as we said at the beginning, you worked in the same factory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was an information specialist, and the Trial Chamber knows about it. What are your -- what kind of comments can you make about him regarding that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I know that Dario, at that time, talked about many problems publicly. He had a lot of understanding for the low-paid workers. He was very courageous during that period, because this was a period that you couldn't speak openly about these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you personally participated in certain protests, that you went out in the streets to protest the delivery of weapons to be used against Republic of Croatia. Do you remember Mr. Kordic from those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. He was among the leaders there. He was -- showed up bare armed and confronted the soldiers who were armed. And one of these convoys that was going into Sarajevo had stopped near my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, in the fall of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You actually personally saw this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were very heated conversation with the people who were escorting the convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: There were these huge rockets which were a part of that convoy, and I was very afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness DE, you occasionally worked with Mr. Kordic, including in the Busovaca municipality in late 1991 and early 1992, but you also followed his public appearances, his press conferences, I assume, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To you, was he a politician or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Dario was primarily a politician. He was a politician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: He conducted press conferences, he was covering the situation, and he tried to define what was going on, especially at the time when we were completely encircled. He wanted the voice of the people who was encircled to be heard around the world, so that the world would know what was going on there, and he also was working on getting humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, madam, are no soldier or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard or seen Mr. Dario Kordic issue any military orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No. I never heard about that. As I said, I had no contact with the military, but from what I did know, I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you heard and followed some of the press conferences. In the area where you live, which is Kaonik, the northern corner of the municipality, what was the TV Busovaca signal? What was the quality of the TV signal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: It was -- the signal was very bad. We -- the sound was a bit better than the image, but it was pretty poor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further north of Kaonik, could -- do you know whether the people there could receive the signal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No. I heard that you couldn't get the signal. It was -- it could only be picked up in the town itself and immediate surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, a little problem with the interpretation. If I understand you correctly, you said that the signal was very weak, that the sound was better, but that occasionally you had neither sound nor image. I think was that omitted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When you followed these press conferences -- I'm sure that you saw more than one -- have you ever heard from Mr. Kordic that he was saying anything bad, that he was saying anything bad about some ethnic group, that he was inciting to violence or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, I did not. He, especially at the time of complete siege, he tried to calm down the people, because there was great mental pressure. Some people were terribly afraid that the lines of defence would collapse, because there were threats that we would all be killed and slaughtered, women and children and all, and people were very concerned. And he acted in such a way in order to turn people towards thinking more positively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if he uttered any critical comments, who was that directed against?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: He spoke critically about the Muslim extremists, especially about the presence of Muslim soldiers who were foreign born, of whom there were many, because people would see them at the lines of defence and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, you know that it has been alleged that Mr. Kordic used Radio Busovaca to issues orders to burn down the village of Loncari specifically on the 16th of April, 1993. Have you ever heard that this was said, and this allegedly was said early in the morning on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: From what I know, Radio Busovaca started its programme at 8.00 in the morning. This was the only radio station we could follow on a regular basis. It started at 8.00 in the morning and worked -- was on the air for four or five hours but it never worked that early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard any such statement on any other media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me conclude this heading on Dario Kordic. What was Mr. Kordic's role in relation -- what was the perception of his role of your neighbours, your fellow citizens?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: We all perceived it as a very positive role. He encouraged people. He directed them to think positively, to believe that they would be able to defend ourselves, that we would survive here, that we shouldn't go anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we talk about it, I assume you know where Mr. Kordic's family lived throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the examples. The entire family of Mr. Kordic lived in Busovaca and Mr. Kordic's wife also showed optimism and said that we should stay here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another area that you were called to give evidence about was -- is that there was a policy which was implemented through the institutions which was a policy which advocated ethnic cleansing of non-Croat ethnic groups from the entire area of Herceg-Bosna. You worked with all these people, you lived with them. Have you ever heard of any official or unofficial campaign of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, I did not. The situation was far more serious. It was a question of life and death. What I am trying to say is that in a way, that was not a priority. The priority was to survive, to organise the life there because we had food shortages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but have you ever heard that there was a policy of persecution of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, I never heard of any such thing, nor was any such thing implemented from what I know. There may have been some individual cases of -- on the part of unthinking individuals who disregarded the government policies and there was a war and the bad side of certain individuals came to the fore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the criminal excesses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, there were some criminal excesses, and I was very sorry for people to whom such things were done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you never heard, but I want your answer on whether any of the officials at higher levels or in public places or in -- through the media ever advocated such a position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had contacts with top leadership in the municipality. They were in charge of the overall policy and, to the contrary, they directed us to treat everybody well and that we should avoid any such -- anything that would lead to such relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their Honours had the opportunity to hear what the census figures were for Busovaca in 1991 and the ratio of Muslims and Croats there, so that is not in dispute. But at the time when the Washington Accords were signed after the cease-fire in 1994, to your knowledge, what were the percentages of territory of the Busovaca municipality under control of the HVO and what percentage was under the ABiH control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: The HVO controlled about 60 per cent and the ABiH about 40 per cent of the overall territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your information, can you tell the Trial Chamber, given your current job, how many Croats and how many Muslims were forced to leave the area of Busovaca municipality, that is, their previous residences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Busovaca municipality, that is about 2.500 of them were forced to leave their homes, both Muslims and Croats. Part of the Croat population, after the situation was calm -- had calmed down returned, and these -- this meant people who were returning to homes that were under the HVO control and those were about 700, but they came back temporarily and they came back to the areas controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm referring to those who lived in the areas affected by the fighting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now just to gain the full picture, you -- do you know the percentage of Muslims who have so far, to date, returned to the Busovaca municipality and what percentage of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Out of these 2.500, the Muslims came back into villages 100 per cent which would be about 1.000. We don't have accurate data for this. They all returned, and all the properties were returned. And in the town, I don't know exactly, about -- about 700, about 50 per cent, already 50 per cent Muslims have returned to the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Far less, about 20 per cent of Croats. Again, I don't have the final figure, but about 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your answers. Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DE, how long have you lived in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Since 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of the use of the barracks, former barracks at Kaonik as a detention facility from at least 1992, possibly earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, I learned about that later, after everything was over when an exchange had taken place. I heard it was a reception centre or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later. Could you say a date, please? When did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I couldn't really pinpoint the date. It could have been a month after the conflicts or I don't really know. After the first conflict -- no, no, it must have been later. It had to be spring, the spring of 1993. But that barracks is completely isolated on a hill. The entrance is on the other side. I can't see it from my house so I couldn't see what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never saw persons during 1992 and 1993 being taken to Kaonik? You never saw that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No. No, I did not. I'm telling you the barracks is on a hill. The entrance is on the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Barracks? You mean the barracks?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted). I worked there prior to 1993. I don't really know about these business deals, that is, I do not know what Vatrostalna did or delivered because I did not work for the commercial department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: So salaries, payments, cashiers, and some of the bookkeeping were kept in Busovaca because a considerable part of that was in Zenica where we had the mainframe computer. So the payments, the analysis of payments was done in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted). Can you give, please, exactly the years from when to when; month, year, month year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: April 1978 to January 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in any type of managerial position when you worked (redacted) or were you just one of the workers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted), and I can't remember really all the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were not a managerial person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your education in Sarajevo as a -- did you branch graduate as an economist or did you just study economics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I graduated in economics in 1978. In four years' time, I graduated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In former communist countries, can you please explain what an economist does. It appears that that was not an uncommon type of area to go into, but its exact function may be less clear to western academics. Can you please explain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: You mean that service which I headed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does an economist do, a graduate economist? What types of -- what is it? Is it a highly-skilled job? Is it math or is it arithmetic? Is it management? What is being an economist. At the time you finished school -- if I may just add this to the question -- it was still the former Yugoslavia. What role could you play in a command economy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I was admitted to the section for analysis and planning. So first we would draw up annual plans, then medium-term plans for the production of fire refraction materials in the plant. The technical service will provide me with information as to what is manufactured, how is it manufactured, what are the costs, so on and so forth. Then we talked about the overall costs, about the money. Then we would try to calculate the prices on the basis of all the input, then to compare the planned price to the market price, and we would try to harmonise the two to somehow -- that is, starting from a unit product. We would then move on to the overall output to establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. I don't think we're being assisted by this. Can we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask just as a final follow question about the nature of the work. Did you ever have the final say in anything or were you just part of a group of people giving input?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I did have a final say when proposing plans or, rather, I would present the plan to the management bodies in the plant, and I would draw up the plan with the help of the technical services, with the production staff; that is, we would draw up plans together. We would all be part of a team. Then the plan would be brought down to the financial plan, and I would present it to the management of the plant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: That was not the name of the department. I was appointed in 1991 to (redacted) (redacted). I was appointed by the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who in the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I'm not objecting to the question, but we should go into private session. But when various jobs of the witness are mentioned, I think that should be struck out from the transcript. That is the only thing I'm worried about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can certainly go around it if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go around it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Okay. The present --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, in order -- may I address the Bench on this point? In order for me to ask about certain aspects of the current work, I don't know how identifiably that would be with the personality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me please, Witness DE, what was your reaction to the burning of the mosque in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: To begin with, I was not told about that, because I wasn't -- because I didn't come to the office for several days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Then when I heard about it -- I don't know. I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: It was -- how shall I explain it? -- next to the old school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see it from your office? Did you have pass it going home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No. No. No, I didn't. It's a completely different part of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to learn that it was gone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Well, simply the story went around town that somebody -- that one night somebody planted some explosive. What else could it be? I don't know. I'm telling you. I don't know. I heard it from other people talking about it. I don't pass -- I don't take that route all that often. There is no reason for me to walk in that direction, so that I did not see that. I only heard it from other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you heard it, did it concern you that an institution as long-standing as a mosque could be the target of an explosion or a burning? What was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time there was destruction of business outlets. There were people with a destructive way of thinking. I don't know how to put it. There was a war going on. It wasn't good. It wasn't good. It's never good to destroy anything. If somebody invested his labour, his effort, and then to bring it down, it's bad, especially if it is a religious object.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kaonik camp, not the barracks any more but the detention centre that was used by the HVO to detain mainly Muslim males of military age, do you know how that camp was supplied with food, where the transportation came from? How did people get into that camp, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't. I have no idea. These are military matters, and I repeat, I simply had nothing to do with military affairs or any information about it. I never received any such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the persons, whose names shall not be mentioned, about whom we talked recently in private session, did any of those persons indicate a time spent in Kaonik? As detainees, not as visitors, as detainees.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without names, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without names, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. It was mentioned on one occasion. I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice a diminution, a reduction in the population of the Muslim community in Busovaca? Did that catch your eye?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, of course. After a large number of displaced persons arrived, especially from the areas of Travnik and Zenica, they had lost their homes, had suffered pressure before they arrived in Busovaca. They came there and brought pressure on the local population to move out or, rather, they were looking for some accommodation for themselves and their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity were these displaced persons that you've just described from Zenica, Travnik? What ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Why, they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything? Were you outraged at the fact that an order to accommodate displaced Croats, the HVO, including Dario Kordic, displaced local Muslims? In fact, there were records of significant numbers of expulsions to accommodate these Croats. How did you view this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't really all that familiar with the problem. It was the social work centre which took place of the displaced persons. I know that they tried to prevail upon the Muslim population and offered them their own homes. I know a man who, because of the frequent pressure by a Zenica man, had to leave his house. He went to Zenica, but before that, he dropped by my place and spent the night at my place with his daughter, telling me that he could not stand the pressure of those displaced persons any more and that he was on his way to exchange, to swap houses. That was, for instance, something that I experienced personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To swap houses with whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: There was a displaced person from Zenica who offered his house. He had already come to Busovaca, and he offered him his own house in Zenica in return, in exchange. I think that there were a number of such agreements. Some were even put down on paper about these exchanges. Some thought that this would be a temporary thing. Some thought this was permanent. But as we know, we know that in wartime this was not a thing that could stand. This would have to be temporary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with Mrs. Neslanovic after she left -- after she stopped coming to work? Have you seen her since 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: After April 1993, I believe I did not see her, and we did not have any conversations. She was an employee and did her job. There were no conversations. Sometimes she would stay behind for overtime because there were incentives for that, but we had no special conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Busovaca, you indicated, was a fairly small location. Did word get back to you about her situation where, in May of 1993, she was the only Muslim left in her neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I did not fully understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because Busovaca is a small enough town for information to pass quickly, or rumour, did you hear about Mrs. Neslanovic being the only Muslim left in her neighbourhood in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: In May 1993, no, because I didn't see her. She did not show up for work so I did not know whether she was still in Busovaca or not because in April, she would still come to work. After that, she stopped, and I did not know whether she was still in Busovaca. In fact, I don't even know exactly where she lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you knew that Croats were moving into Muslim homes. You did not hear then that she was given five minutes to leave her house in which she had lived for years and years and vacate so that a Croat family could move in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No. I hear this from you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the deaths of two Muslim males whose names I shall give you. One is a Mirsad Delija and the other one was Ibro Hodzic, both Busovaca residents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, I know about it. I learned about it later. And I regretted that I knew Mr. Hodzic because he was a municipal employee. Mr. Delija, I did not know, but I subsequently learned that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you learn about the death of Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I heard that he was attacked in his apartment and that they wanted to evict him, but these were rumours. I am not sure who it was. I know no closer details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Very superficially. I'm not sure that I would recognise her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was a municipal employee in the same building in which you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of management, did you pay a condolence call?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: As I did not know the lady, and I did not know where they lived. And probably, at that time, I wasn't even working. I wasn't coming to work, because I assumed this was after the first conflict. Times were difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer is no, you did not pay a condolence call?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, I did not, because I wasn't that close to the family at all. I only knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you know about the death of Mr. Delija whom you said you did not know personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I also heard that some men had broken into his apartment or wherever he lived. That they shot, because he wouldn't open up, but I did not know the man or where his -- where he lived or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what, if any, events may have occurred in Busovaca the night after his death or the same night of his death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No, I don't recall. I think that at the time, I wasn't coming to work and my home is about five kilometres from Busovaca, and I don't know at all what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if I were to suggest to you that there were massive explosions in Muslim shops, are you suggesting that the sound of a number of explosions would not carry to the area of Busovaca near Kaonik where you lived? Are you really telling us that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Kaonik is five kilometres away, and it's a hilly terrain, so you definitely would not have heard it in Kaonik. But, as I said, at the time, I came to work very infrequently and I noticed that there were -- that all the business premises were vandalised, that they were looted, but it wasn't restricted only to Muslim business premises. The scene of the crime rate had definitely risen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know it wasn't restricted to Muslim business premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Well, I recall when I would come to work occasionally that all store shops were either boarded up or vandalised, that there were no -- there was no goods in them, that everything had been taken away. It looked horrible. How should I describe it? I saw -- I don't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you name the Croat stores or the Croat shops, the businesses that were vandalised the names of the owners, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Well, there were some state-owned premises like the department store that was all vandalised and everything had been taken away. I don't know what shops specifically these were. There were -- there was a company which -- there was a state-owned company, I don't know if it was a Muslim-majority owned. It was socially-owned as it was called then, a company, and their outlet was one of those, but I remember that there was no merchandise. It was all gaping, it was ghostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something about the educational system. You commented that for the school year 1992-93, we eliminated the old Yugoslavia Serb-dominated socialist school programme and you taught classes based on a curriculum based from Mostar. Why Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: The HVO government was established in Mostar, and it tried to -- it made attempts to link up to the municipal governments. There were no other curricula offered. This one was offered, but a possibility was left open that certain agreements be worked out with the local principals so that the Muslim and Croat authors would be included, but it was left for people to make agreements about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have children. What Muslim historians, authors, points of culture, were included? Please specify.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but for instance, Mak Dizdar. I personally was not involved in the details of these curricula. The education specialists, the principals, were involved in this, but the door was open to agreements. I don't recall very much, and I did not -- I did not scrutinise it that much. That was left to the educators, to the teachers in schools to deal with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there no textbooks available from Sarajevo or was there, if you know, was there a difference in the curriculum that was being taught in the schools there? I realise that both places were under siege, but was there a difference in the curriculum? As a mother, what would you expect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: There is a number of questions here. I will -- first the textbooks from Sarajevo. Those had Yugoslav in orientation, they were not Bosnian in their character. And it was under siege, the biggest printing plant was all blown up, and I believe that all the textbooks have been scattered, taken away, and you couldn't count on textbooks from Sarajevo and there was no curriculum coming out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had indicated difficulties in having pay met and generally financial difficulties. Now, it was certainly easier for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna because of the generous and very regular support coming from Croatia. Was that support not given to other parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I don't know where it went regarding the education. Yes, some textbooks, some teaching aids were received for free. I don't know about other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know about other areas where Croatian assistance went to, is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just one or two more questions. If you'll give me a minute, please. You indicated that you had regular contact with Dario Kordic during the time you worked in Busovaca. What was your observation as to how often he left Busovaca during the period 1991 through -- and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: After the episodes with the barracks and the air raids, there was no -- this Secretariat for Defence no longer existed, and we had to move out of the second floor because it was too dangerous to stay there. So nobody was there any longer. And I saw Mr. Kordic very rarely, first, because I was not coming to work regularly; and second, he went around to gather information and attend press conferences, and I saw him only infrequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw Mr. Kordic before seeing him as an accused in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I cannot recall, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start from the end. We talked about this education. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after its independence was declared, a new school curriculum for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was ever adopted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Your Honours, such curriculum was never adopted or never implemented in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the schools used textbooks of the former school system from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina when it was still part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last question, if I remember correctly: At the municipal level there was a flexible curriculum which was not to be in favour or disfavour to any of the communities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, and it was then to be worked out in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could I have Z175? Do you have it perhaps in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document was mentioned several times. Can you please read item 1 on it? What does item 1 say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: "In the temporary provisional" -- [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You don't have to read it through, but would you agree with me that these decisions demonstrated -- they are issued temporarily, until the municipal -- proper municipal bodies were established after the agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes. It was very temporary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question was why did such a document did not come to Sarajevo, and my question to you would be: Did the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina function in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: What should I tell you? It is absurd to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, it was not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No. Nothing functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, a seal was mentioned, and it states "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mostar 1." Do you know whether Mr. Kordic ever worked in Mostar in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't believe that he worked there. I think this was all very temporary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. One quick question about telephones. The question was whether you had a telephone line in your office in 1992 and 1993. My question to you would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleagues are pointing to -- that what the witness had read was not recorded in the transcript, and I didn't want to put it on the ELMO for fear of revealing something that was under protection. So maybe myself or the witness could read it over again so that it be made part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please read it out slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: "In the provisional administrative executive government of the -- Busovaca, the decisions of the heads of departments shall be issued until the completion of the procedure of the municipal Croatian Defence Council."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that we got it now. Thank you. I think we will have to ask the Translation Department for a correction. But let's move on to the phones. Could you talk to anybody from your office throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Europe, and the rest of the world?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: (redacted). So it was very dangerous to stay there. And I believe I only stayed there for several hours during that year, because we all moved down because of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if you needed to phone, to make a telephone call, would you have had free telephone access in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: No. These phone lines were in -- very questionable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had some questions about this attendance record, but I think you answered all the questions there. You gave a personal example. You said that person, a Muslim, was forced to exchange houses with a Croat from Zenica. These were individual cases. But at the municipal level, did HVO -- and this would then involve Dario Kordic, I think that is the gist of the question -- did they implement any policy of forced resettlement of Muslims from Busovaca to any other areas? 17 A. As far as I know, no. The main pressure was from those displaced persons coming mostly from the Travnik, Zenica and other regions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You talked about Mr. Hodzic's death, and you said what you knew about it. My question is: After Mr. Hodzic's death, did you see on television Mr. Dario Kordic expressing condolences and condemning this event? Did you have an opportunity to see that on television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I saw a programme of that content. As I said, the signal was very poor where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the beginning, there was -- there were quite a few questions about the employment of Muslims after the implementation of the Dayton Accords. I think that there was some misunderstanding there. The current municipal council is composed of members from both ethnic groups. Who reached the agreement that these people worked there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the agreement was reached by the governing parties, that is, the parties who had won at the elections. The representatives of both parties agreed that this municipal council be formed and specified its composition and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This is not to -- just sheer employment policy, this was a result of the agreement of two parties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness DE, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, you've got two more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have two witnesses, and as far as the Defence is concerned, they may both be examined tomorrow, but if necessary, we can move one to the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I hope very much we can deal with them both tomorrow. They're fairly short witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll make sure that we finish them tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half past nine tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 3.59 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of May, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
